title: 22. Interview: Design WhatsApp
summary: Interview Q&A for Design WhatsApp — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design WhatsApp interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **WebSocket vs MQTT vs HTTP long-polling**: WebSocket is bidirectional and lowest latency (~50 ms) but requires sticky sessions; MQTT is lighter on battery (publish/subscribe model) but adds broker overhead; long-polling is simplest but high latency. We pick WebSocket for phones on WiFi/cellular, MQTT for low-end devices.
- **Erlang vs Go vs Java**: Erlang has the best concurrency model (millions of processes, hot code reload, supervision trees) — WhatsApp's proven choice. Go is simpler to hire for and has good performance. Java is heavy on memory. We pick Erlang for connection servers (matching WhatsApp's real architecture) and Go for stateless routing services.
- **Pairwise encryption vs group sender keys**: pairwise is O(N²) keys per group message; sender keys are O(N) — 1 000× savings in a 1 024-member group. We use Signal's sender key for groups.
- **Store all messages forever vs TTL**: forever means storage grows unbounded (43 TB/year metadata, 3.6 PB/year media). WhatsApp chose "media deleted after download" originally; multi-device forced them to retain media for 90 days. We retain messages indefinitely (user choice) but tier media to Glacier after 90 days.
- **Push notifications vs always-on sockets**: always-on drains battery; push wakes the app on demand but adds latency. Hybrid: socket open when app is foregrounded, push when backgrounded.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why does WhatsApp use Erlang for its connection servers?
**Answer:** Erlang/OTP was designed by Ericsson for telecom switches with three properties that match WhatsApp's needs perfectly. (1) **Massive concurrency**: Erlang processes are lightweight (~2 KB stack), so a single node holds millions of connections — WhatsApp has measured ~2 M per node. (2) **Fault tolerance**: the "let it crash" philosophy + supervision trees mean a buggy message handler crashes one process, not the whole node; supervisors restart it cleanly. (3) **Hot code loading**: Erlang can upgrade code without dropping connections — critical for a 24/7 service with 2 B users. Go's goroutines (~8 KB) are 4× heavier, and Go lacks hot reloading. Java's thread model is heavier still. The trade-off: Erlang is harder to hire for and has a smaller ecosystem, but for connection-heavy real-time systems it remains the gold standard.
**Visual:**
```
Erlang process: ~2 KB stack, millions per node, "let it crash" + supervisor
Go goroutine:   ~8 KB stack, hundreds of thousands per node
Java thread:    ~512 KB-1 MB stack, thousands per node
```

### Q2. How does the Signal Protocol achieve forward secrecy and post-compromise security?
**Answer:** Signal uses the **Double Ratchet** algorithm. Each message uses a new symmetric key derived from a chain. (1) **Forward secrecy**: keys are derived via a one-way function (HMAC) and the previous key is deleted after use — if an attacker compromises the current key, they cannot decrypt past messages. (2) **Post-compromise security**: a Diffie-Hellman ratchet generates new shared secrets on every message round-trip — if an attacker compromises one key, the next DH exchange "heals" the channel and future messages are secure again. Combined with X3DH for initial key agreement (using one-time pre-keys), the protocol ensures that even if the server is fully compromised, only the sender and recipient can read messages. WhatsApp, Signal, and Facebook Messenger's Secret Conversations all use this.
**Visual:**
```
Initial: X3DH -> shared_secret
  |
  v
Chain key K1 -> K2 -> K3 -> ... (one-way, old keys deleted)
  |       |       |
  v       v       v
Msg1    Msg2    Msg3
  (forward secrecy: compromising K3 doesn't reveal K1)

DH ratchet on every reply:
  K3 --DH--> new_shared -> K4 -> K5 ...
  (post-compromise security: compromise heals after next DH)
```

### Q3. How does group E2EE work without N² pairwise encryption?
**Answer:** Signal's **Sender Keys** protocol. Each group member, for each other member, establishes a pairwise secure channel (via X3DH). When Alice first sends to a group, she generates a ChainKey, encrypts it with each pairwise channel, and sends it to all members — this is a one-time setup. For subsequent messages, Alice uses her ChainKey to derive message keys (one per message) and broadcasts the same ciphertext to everyone. Each recipient has Alice's ChainKey (received once) and can derive the same message keys to decrypt. Cost: O(N) setup, O(1) per message — vs O(N²) if every message were pairwise encrypted. For a 1 024-member group, this is 1 000× cheaper. When a member leaves, the sender rotates the ChainKey (via the same pairwise channel) — leaving members can't read new messages.
**Visual:**
```
Setup (once per sender per group):
  Alice -> pairwise E2EE -> each member: "here's my ChainKey"
Per message:
  Alice: derive msg_key = HMAC(ChainKey, seq); encrypt(msg, msg_key)
  Alice broadcasts ciphertext + seq to all members
  Each member: derive same msg_key, decrypt
Leaving member: Alice rotates ChainKey, re-distributes to remaining
```

### Q4. How do read receipts work, and how do you handle the "disable read receipts" feature?
**Answer:** When a user opens a conversation, the client tracks the highest `message_id` read and sends a `read` receipt to the sender's devices. The sender's client shows blue ✓✓. To "disable read receipts": the client still processes incoming messages normally but does NOT send `read` receipts to other users. However, for the user's own multi-device sync (their phone and web client must show consistent ✓✓ state), the router still routes read receipts between the user's own devices. Subtle catch: if Alice disables receipts and reads Bob's message, Bob doesn't get blue ticks — but if Alice's web client also has the message, the web client learns Alice read it via the multi-device sync. Trade-off: cannot fully hide read state from your own multi-device. Real-world: WhatsApp behaves exactly this way.
**Visual:**
```
Alice reads Bob's message:
  Phone client -> router -> "read receipt" -> Bob (if Alice's receipts enabled)
                              |
                              +-> Alice's other devices (always, for sync)

Alice disabled receipts:
  Phone client -> router -> "read receipt" -> Alice's other devices ONLY
                          (no receipt to Bob)
```

### Q5. How does presence scale to 2 B users without overwhelming Redis?
**Answer:** Three optimizations. (1) **Heartbeat batching**: clients heartbeat every 30 s, but the connection server batches heartbeats per second and updates Redis in bulk (one MSET per second per server). This reduces Redis QPS from 600 M to ~50 k. (2) **Subscription filtering**: a user only sees presence for their contacts. Each user subscribes to a Redis pub/sub channel `presence_updates:{user_id}` — only contacts publish there. Without filtering, every status change would fan out to billions of subscribers. (3) **Tiered storage**: hot users (recently active) in Redis, cold users (offline > 7 days) fall back to Postgres `last_seen_at`. Trade-off: presence is eventually consistent — a "user online" can lag 30 s behind reality. Battery cost: 30 s heartbeat is a deliberate trade-off vs 5 s (more accurate but drains battery 6× faster).
**Visual:**
```
600M users * 1 heartbeat/30s = 20M QPS naive
  |
  +--> batch per second: 50k QPS to Redis
  +--> only publish to contacts: ~100 subs/user
  +--> tier: hot in Redis, cold in Postgres
```

### Q6. How do you handle message ordering in a conversation?
**Answer:** Each conversation has a sequence number generator. We use a Snowflake-style generator sharded by `conversation_id % N` (say N=64) — so different conversations don't contend for the same sequence generator, but messages within a conversation are strictly monotonic. The router assigns the sequence server-side (not client-side) to prevent client clock skew from causing out-of-order messages. Clients display messages ordered by sequence number, not arrival time. Edge case: if the network reorders messages in transit (rare with TCP, but possible across retries), the client buffers and orders by sequence before displaying. For groups, the same generator serves all members — they all see the same sequence numbers, ensuring consistent ordering across the group. Trade-off: sequence generation is a single point per conversation — mitigated by sharding and by making the generator fast (Snowflake ~1 M IDs/s per shard).
**Visual:**
```
Conversation 12345 -> shard = 12345 % 64 = 57
Shard 57 sequence: ... seq=42, seq=43, seq=44 ...
  |
  v
All recipients display by sequence (not arrival time)
  -> consistent order across devices and group members
```

### Q7. Why doesn't the server store messages in plaintext, and what can the server still see?
**Answer:** The server cannot decrypt messages because only sender and recipient hold the ratchet keys — the server stores only ciphertext blobs. However, the server must store some metadata to route messages: sender user ID, recipient user ID, message size, timestamp, and message ID. This metadata is enough to build a "social graph" (who talks to whom, when, how often). WhatsApp minimizes this: messages are delivered and the routing metadata can be ephemeral (deleted after delivery), though the inbox copy must persist until the user deletes it. For stronger privacy, the Signal Protocol supports "sealed sender" — the sender's identity is encrypted inside the message envelope, so the server only knows "a message was sent to recipient B" without knowing who sent it. Trade-off: sealed sender makes spam detection harder. Real-world: Signal uses sealed sender; WhatsApp exposes sender to the server for spam/abuse detection.
**Visual:**
```
Server stores:
  - sender_id, recipient_id, timestamp, size (metadata, visible)
  - ciphertext (encrypted, NOT decryptable by server)
  - media_url, media_key (encrypted media, key only on devices)

Server does NOT see:
  - message content (text)
  - media content (image/video)
  - optional: sender identity (with sealed sender)
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A user reports messages arriving out of order in a group chat. How do you debug?
**Answer:** First, gather details: which group, which member, what device, what timestamps. Check the sequence numbers assigned by the router — are they monotonic? If yes, the issue is client-side: the client is displaying by arrival time instead of sequence. If sequence numbers are not monotonic, the sequence generator shard for that conversation is misbehaving — check if two shards are serving the same conversation (sharding bug) or if the Snowflake clock went backward. Next, check Cassandra writes — were they all successful? A retry after a failed write can produce a duplicate with a later sequence but earlier content. Check the fanout path — did the router fan out to all members in the same batch, or did some members receive via Kafka lag? Finally, check client clock skew — if the client displays by local timestamp instead of server sequence, two devices with skewed clocks will show different orders. Fix: ensure client always sorts by server-assigned sequence number, never local arrival time.
**Visual:**
```
Out-of-order reported
  |
  +--> check router sequence numbers (monotonic?)
  |       yes -> client displaying wrong field (arrival vs sequence)
  |       no  -> shard bug or clock skew in Snowflake
  +--> check Cassandra writes (duplicates from retries?)
  +--> check fanout (Kafka lag for some members?)
  +--> check client clock skew (sort by seq, not local ts)
```

### Q2. A group with 1 024 members is causing high CPU on the router every time one member sends. What's the bottleneck and fix?
**Answer:** Bottleneck: 1 024 fanouts per message. Each fanout involves (1) a Redis lookup for the recipient's connection server, (2) a delivery call to that server, (3) a Cassandra write to the recipient's inbox. At 1 message/second from the sender, that's 1 024 Redis lookups + 1 024 deliveries + 1 024 Cassandra writes per second — saturating the router. Fix: (1) **Batch fanout via Kafka** — publish one message to a per-group Kafka topic; connection servers consume in parallel and deliver to their local sockets. (2) **Skip inbox writes for online recipients** — write to Cassandra lazily only on disconnect (the connection server's local queue holds the message until ack). (3) **Rate-limit the sender** — cap to 10 messages/minute in groups > 100 members (legitimate users won't hit this; spammers will). (4) **Shard the group** — for very large groups (>1 024), consider a tree-based fanout where regional hubs aggregate. Real-world: Discord uses Kafka-based fanout for servers with up to 100 k members.
**Visual:**
```
Before: sender -> router -> 1024 Redis lookups + 1024 deliveries + 1024 Cassandra writes
After:
  sender -> router -> publish to Kafka topic "group-{gid}"
                            |
   connection servers consume in parallel --> deliver to local sockets
   Cassandra write only on disconnect (lazy)
   Rate-limit sender to 10 msg/min in large groups
```

### Q3. A user's phone is stolen. How do you revoke the device without breaking their other devices?
**Answer:** Two paths. (1) **User-initiated**: from a linked device (web), the user calls `POST /devices/{stolen_id}/revoke`. The router deletes the device row in Postgres, invalidates all its pre-keys, sends a "remote wipe" command to the stolen device (if it's still online — the connection server pushes a control message that tells the client to delete local data and disconnect). (2) **Server-initiated** (if the user has no other linked device): the user must verify identity via SMS code to a new phone, then call the same revoke API. For the user's other devices: nothing changes — they keep their keys and connections. For the stolen device's recipients: they need to know the device is gone so they don't encrypt to it. Solution: the key server marks the device's prekeys as `revoked`; senders fetch the recipient's prekey bundle before each new session and see only active devices. Trade-off: messages already encrypted to the stolen device before revocation are lost (can't be delivered) — but that's the security goal.
**Visual:**
```
Stolen phone:
  Web client -> POST /devices/{stolen_id}/revoke
    |
    +--> Postgres: mark device revoked, delete prekeys
    +--> Push "remote wipe" to stolen device (if online)
    +--> Key server: prekeys marked revoked
    +--> Senders fetching prekey bundle -> only see active devices
    +--> Other devices: unaffected, keep their keys
```

### Q4. Messages are lagging 30 seconds in a single region during a peak event (NYE). What do you do?
**Answer:** Three actions. (1) **Scale out connection servers** — auto-scale group adds 2× capacity; new nodes join the LB pool and start accepting new connections. (2) **Check Cassandra write latency** — if writes are p99 > 500 ms, the cluster is saturated; bump the replication factor's consistency level from QUORUM to LOCAL_ONE (faster writes, slight risk of stale reads — acceptable during spike). (3) **Shed non-critical traffic** — disable typing indicators and presence updates for the duration (they're "best effort" anyway). (4) **Check Kafka** — if consumer lag is growing, scale Flink task slots and Kafka consumer parallelism. (5) **Pre-warm** — for predictable events like NYE, pre-scale 30 min before midnight. (6) **Communicate** — show a "messages may be delayed" banner in the app. Long-term: capacity plan for 5× average, not 2× — NYE spikes are 3-5× normal in messaging apps. Real-world: WhatsApp saw 18 B messages on NYE 2020 — they pre-scale aggressively.
**Visual:**
```
NYE spike: 5x normal = 6M msgs/s
  |
  +--> scale out connection servers 2x
  +--> Cassandra: QUORUM -> LOCAL_ONE (faster writes)
  +--> shed typing indicators + presence updates
  +--> Kafka: scale Flink task slots
  +--> pre-warm 30min before midnight
  +--> banner: "messages may be delayed"
```

### Q5. A user complains they can't see a contact's "last seen" anymore. What changed?
**Answer:** Three possibilities. (1) **Privacy setting**: the contact changed their privacy to "hide last seen from everyone" or "hide from non-contacts" — WhatsApp exposes this in Settings → Privacy → Last Seen. If the user is not in the contact's address book, they won't see it. (2) **Blocking**: the contact blocked the user — both last seen and online status disappear. (3) **Bug**: presence service lag, or the user's subscription to the contact's presence channel expired (Redis TTL). To debug: check the user's privacy settings (no, it's the contact's settings, not theirs), check if the user is in the contact's address book, check Redis for the contact's presence key, check the user's subscription channel. Fix: if it's a privacy setting, communicate to the user (we can't override the contact's choice); if it's a bug, refresh the subscription. Real-world: this is one of the most common WhatsApp support tickets.
**Visual:**
```
"Can't see last seen"
  |
  +--> contact's privacy: hide from everyone / non-contacts?
  +--> contact blocked the user?
  +--> bug: presence subscription expired (Redis TTL)?
  |       |
  |       +--> refresh subscription, re-fetch presence
  +--> if privacy/block: communicate (can't override)
```

### Q6. The Cassandra cluster is at 80% disk — messages are piling up. How do you reduce storage growth?
**Answer:** Multi-pronged. (1) **TTL on messages**: add a `default_time_to_live` of 1 year on the messages table — old messages auto-expire. But this breaks the "messages forever" expectation. Compromise: TTL only for users who opt-in to "auto-delete after 1 year" (à la WhatsApp's disappearing messages). (2) **Media offloading**: move media to S3 + lifecycle to Glacier (already done). (3) **Compaction strategy**: switch from `SizeTieredCompactionStrategy` (default) to `TimeWindowCompactionStrategy` for time-series data — 50% reduction in disk usage. (4) **Compression**: enable LZ4 or Zstandard compression on the messages table — 2-4× reduction. (5) **Archive old messages**: a background job moves messages older than 1 year to a colder Cassandra keyspace (cheaper nodes, slower reads). (6) **User-driven deletion**: encourage users to delete old chats; offer "delete messages older than X" in settings. Real-world: WhatsApp moved to a custom storage stack that combines Cassandra-like design with their own optimizations.
**Visual:**
```
80% disk:
  +--> TTL 1y for opt-in "disappearing messages"
  +--> compaction: STCS -> TWCS (-50% disk)
  +--> compression: LZ4/Zstd (-2 to 4x)
  +--> archive >1y to cold keyspace (cheaper nodes)
  +--> media already on S3 + Glacier
  +--> user deletion ("delete older than X")
```

### Q7. A government requests message content for a criminal investigation. What can you provide?
**Answer:** Because of E2EE, the server cannot decrypt message content — it stores only ciphertext. So we can comply with the legal request by providing: (1) metadata — sender, recipient, timestamp, message size, for the specified time window. (2) The ciphertext blobs themselves — but without the ratchet keys (held only on devices), they're computationally infeasible to decrypt. (3) Group membership records — who was in which group and when. (4) Account information — phone number, registration date, last seen. We cannot provide: message content, media content, contact lists (unless stored on server). The government would need to compel the user's device (e.g., seize the phone and force unlock) to get plaintext — which is outside our control. This is the core privacy promise of E2EE and the subject of ongoing debates (e.g., the UK Online Safety Bill's impact on WhatsApp). Real-world: WhatsApp has shut down service in jurisdictions requiring backdoors.
**Visual:**
```
Gov request: "give us Alice's messages to Bob from Jan 2025"
  |
  +--> CAN provide:
        - metadata (sender, recipient, ts, size)
        - ciphertext (undecryptable without device keys)
        - group membership, account info
  +--> CANNOT provide:
        - message content (no key)
        - media content (encrypted with client media key)
  +--> Gov must compel device (seize phone) to get plaintext
```
